18. MALE AND FEMALE STERILISATION

•Prevalence of male sterilization was higher in more developed regions whereas the prevalence of female sterilization was higher in developing regions.
•Legal advice should be sought if there is any doubt as to whether a person has the mental capacity to consent to a procedure that will permanently remove their fertility.
•Written consent should be obtained from individuals wishing to undergo vasectomy or laparoscopic or hysteroscopic tubal occlusion.

Pre-sterilization assessment:

•All verbal advice must be supported by accurate, impartial, printed or recorded information.
•Advice post-vasectomy: Men who have undergone vasectomy should be provided with a post- procedural information leaflet that outlines appropriate self-care and instructions.
•Advice post-tubal occlusion: Women should be provided with information about the method of tubal occlusion undertaken and: of any complications.
•Additional contraception: Individuals who have undergone vasectomy should be informed of the need to use additional contraception until sterility is confirmed.
•Regret: Additional care must be taken when counselling individuals under the age of 30 years or individuals without children who request sterilization. If tubal occlusion is performed at the same time as a caesarean section, counselling and agreement should be given at least 2 weeks in advance of the procedure.

 

Vasectomy:

•Under local Anaesthesia wherever possible.
•LA is ➡️ infiltration of the subcuticular tissue ➡️ direct injection to the vas deferens.
•Cauterization followed by division of the vas deferens, with or without excision, is associated with the lowest likelihood of early recanalization (failure) when compared to other occlusion techniques.
•Clips are not recommended for occluding the vas deferens as their use is associated with a potentially high failure rate when compared to other occlusion methods.

Post-vasectomy semen analysis:

•Post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA) should be carried out to identify early failure.
•If motile sperm are observed in a fresh sample 7 months post-procedure, the vasectomy should be considered a failure.

Intraoperative complications:

•Bleeding: Health professionals should cauterize or suture any bleeding peri vasal and subdermal blood vessels to ensure haemostasis.
•Pain: Health professionals should consider the administration of additional Anaesthesia/analgesia.
•Infection: The routine use of prophylactic antibiotics is not recommended prior to vasectomy.
•Early failure: Clinicians should modify their technique if overall failure attributable to technical failure, recanalization and non-compliance with additional contraception is more than 1%.

Long-term complications

•The contraceptive failure rate should be quoted as approximately 1 in 2000 (0.05%).

 

•Interventions for chronic post-vasectomy pain: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and treatment to alleviate neuropathic pain are common first-line treatment options for chronic post-vasectomy pain (CPVP).
•Prostate and testicular cancer: There is no evidence of an increase in testicular cancers associated with vasectomy. The weak association observed in some studies between vasectomy and prostatic cancer is unlikely to be causal.
•Reversal: Vasectomy reversal involves complex surgery that can result in high postoperative patency rates, but may not result in pregnancy or a return to fertility.

Tubal occlusion:

⇨Culdoscopy should not be used as a method of approach for sterilization.
⇨The laparoscopic approach to the fallopian tubes is quicker to perform and results in less minor morbidity compared to mini-laparotomy.
⇨All women should be informed of the risks associated with laparoscopy and when this may proceed to laparotomy. In some cases, laparoscopy/laparotomy may be contraindicated and consideration should be given to other methods.
⇨Occlusion methods:
•Ligation:

Any effective surgical or mechanical method of tubal occlusion can be used when mini laparotomy the method of approach for an interval sterilization.

•Clips:

For postpartum sterilization, both Filshie clips and modified Pomeroy technique are effective. Filshie clip application is quicker to perform.

•Mechanical occlusion

of the fallopian tubes by Filshie clips should be the method of choice for laparoscopic tubal occlusion.

 

 

 

Excluding pregnancy prior to surgery:

•A pregnancy test must be performed before sterilization to exclude the possibility of a preexisting pregnancy. However, a negative test result does not exclude the possibility of a luteal phase pregnancy.
•Tubal occlusion can be performed at any time during the menstrual cycle, providing that the woman has a negative pregnancy test and is not at risk of luteal-phase pregnancy [unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI) in the past 3 weeks]. If this is not the case, the procedure should be deferred and contraception used until at least 3 weeks from the last instance of UPSI.

Stopping contraception after laparoscopic tubal occlusion:

•CHC, the POP or non-hormonal contraception should be advised to continue their contraceptive method for at least 7 days after laparoscopic sterilization.
•If the progestogen only injectable or implant is being used, laparoscopic tubal occlusion can be carried out at any time during the period of licensed use without the need for additional contraception.
•The progestogen-only implant can be removed at the time of the procedure or any time following laparoscopic tubal occlusion.
•If a Cu-lUD or LNG-IUS is in situ prior to sterilization, this should be retained and removed at least 1 week after dafter laparoscopic tubal occlusion.
⇨Failure of tubal occlusion
•The ends of a fallopian tube can recanalize
•A fistula can develop at the occluded portion of the tube
•There may be incomplete occlusion of the tube
•There may be slippage of the occlusive device
•The occlusive device can be placed on the wrong anatomical structure

 

Failure Rate: estimated to be 1 in 200. Filshie clip, suggests a failure rate of 2–3 per 1000 procedures at 10 years

⇨Hysteroscopic sterilization:
•There is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of oral NSAIDs or intravenous sedation for hysteroscopic sterilization.
•The incidence of unsuccessful placement. of intra-fallopian implants. Is reported as ranging between 0 » and 19%.
•Following sterilization via hysteroscopy and the insertion of intra-fallopian micro-inserts, additional contraception must be used until either successful insert placement and/or tubal occlusion are confirmed.
•Intraoperative complications with tubal micro-inserts: a low level of intraoperative complications in a minority of patients.
•Postoperative complications of hysteroscopic sterilization: with a low level of postoperative complications.
•A confirmatory imaging test should be undertaken 3 months after the insertion of intra-fallopian micro-inserts. This may be via X-ray or transvaginal hysterosalpingogram (HSG) in selected patients where X-ray/TVUSS cannot confirm satisfactory placement.

Confirmatory Imaging Post Female Sterilization with Micro insert

Radiological follow-up

In the UK and Europe, the placement of an Essure® device can be followed up by performing a pelvic ultrasound scan at 3 months post-procedure.

In the USA, it was mandatory until recently to perform HSG (hysterosalpingogram) to confirm device position and tubal occlusion 3 months after the procedure. In difficult cases or where the device is not easily visualized, a modified HSG technique is used, in which contrast media is instilled gently to allow cornual filling.

Four radiographic markers are used as landmarks to confirm satisfactory location and tubal occlusion. Satisfactory location is defined as having less than 50% of the inner coil trailing into the uterine cavity or when the proximal marker of the inner coil is 30 mm or closer from where the contrast fills the uterine cornua.

The FDA approved transvaginal ultrasound in as a confirmation test to confirm tubal occlusion in the USA.

The Essure® device is magnetic resonance-conditional, meaning a woman with an Essure® device can undergo MRI scanning with static magnetic field of 3 tesla or less and maximum spatial gradient of magnetic field of 720 gauss/cm or less.

Long-term complications of female’s sterilization:

•Ovarian cancer: protective effect against developing ovarian cancer that persists over time
•Breast cancer: no available evidence of an association between tubal occlusion and breast cancer risk.
•Cervical and endometrial cancer: no association between tubal occlusion and cervical or endometrial cancer risk.
•Others: no evidence that tubal occlusion results in significant changes to hormone levels. Evidence suggests that there is an association between tubal occlusion and an increased risk of subsequent hysterectomy but there is no evidence of causation.
